questions.:question/problem: The rate at which a liquid cools is proportional to the difference between its temperature and the temperature of its surroundings. Let $T(t)$ be the temperature of the liquid in degrees Celsius, and let $t>0$ be the time in minutes. If the temperature of the surroundings is ${25}^{∘}\text{C},$ which differential equation could be used to model the temperature of the liquid? Assume that $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.
questions.:question/worked-solution:
Newton's law of cooling states that the rate at which the temperature $T(t)$ of a body changes is proportional to the difference between its temperature and its surroundings. Therefore, we have the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-{T}_{S}),
$$

where ${T}_{S}$ is the temperature of the surroundings, and $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, ${T}_{S}={25}^{∘}\text{C},$ and we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-25).
$$

canonical_example.:question/problem: A loaf of bread just taken out of the oven has a temperature of $180^{\circ}\textrm{C}.$ After placing it on the table, the temperature $T(t)$ of the bread decreases at a rate that obeys Newton's law of cooling. Here, $T$ is measured in degrees Celsius, and $t > 0$ is the time in minutes. If the room temperature is $25^{\circ}\textrm{C},$ which differential equation could be used to model the bread's temperature? Assume that $k > 0$ is a constant of proportionality.
canonical_example.:question/worked-solution:
Newton's law of cooling states that the rate at which the temperature $T(t)$ of a body changes is proportional to the difference between its temperature and its surroundings. Therefore, we have the differential equation

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d T}{\textrm d t} = -k(T - T_S),
$$

where $T_S$ is the temperature of the surroundings, and $k > 0$ is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, $T_S = 25^{\circ}\textrm{C},$ and we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d T}{\textrm d t} = -k(T - 25).
$$
